opus-5.5.text:
I think the reward function is really a very lossy compression of what you actually want. When you sit down to write one, you have this rich, fuzzy picture in your head — the behavior should be safe, it should be efficient, it should look natural, it shouldn't exploit weird corners of the environment — and then you have to squeeze all of that into a single scalar. Something always gets lost in that squeeze, and the agent is extremely good at finding exactly the part that got lost.

That's the classic reward hacking story. In my experience, especially in robotics, you write what seems like a perfectly reasonable reward — say, move the object toward the goal — and the policy discovers it can flip the object, or vibrate in place, or exploit a physics glitch in simulation. The agent isn't being adversarial; it's just optimizing exactly what you said rather than what you meant. So I've come to see reward design less as specifying a goal and more as an iterative conversation with the optimizer. You write a reward, you watch what comes out, you realize what you forgot to say, and you patch it. A lot of practical RL is honestly this loop of reward shaping, and it takes a lot of human intuition and time.

That's partly why I've gotten interested in alternatives, or at least complements. One direction is learning from demonstrations or preferences — instead of writing down the objective, you show the agent examples or tell it which of two behaviors you prefer, and let it infer the reward. Humans are often much better at recognizing good behavior than at articulating it. Another direction that's become exciting recently is using large language models or vision-language models to help — either to write reward code from a natural-language description, or to act as a judge that scores behavior. That moves the interface closer to how people actually communicate intent: through language and examples, not through hand-tuned coefficients.

But I don't think any of these fully escape the core problem. Whether it's a hand-written reward, a learned reward model, or an LLM judge, there's still a proxy sitting between your true intent and the optimizer, and strong enough optimization will find the gaps in that proxy. So for me the deeper question is how to keep the human in the loop in a scalable way — how to make it cheap for people to notice when the agent is doing the wrong thing and correct it. I think of the reward not as a one-shot specification, but as an evolving, ongoing communication channel between the person and the agent.

r001.rationale: It describes the reward as an evolving communication channel between the person and agent for conveying intent and intended behavior.

r002.rationale: It does not state that verifiable tasks can communicate good performance without an explicit reward function.

r003.rationale: It says humans can recognize preferred behavior and that reward design uses intuition, but does not state that distinguishing good from bad behavior requires tacit human common sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the first thing I'd say is that a reward function is a terrible communication channel, and most of the craft in this field is about accepting that and working around it.

When I write a reward function, I'm compressing an intention that lives in my head, with all its context and exceptions, into a scalar. And the agent doesn't see my intention. It only sees the scalar. So whatever gap exists between what I meant and what I wrote, the optimizer will find that gap, because that's literally its job. People call this reward hacking, but I think the framing is a bit unfair to the agent. It did exactly what I asked. I just asked for the wrong thing.

So in practice I think about it in three layers. The first is: what is the outcome I actually care about, stated as plainly as possible? Not "walk forward," but "get to the other side of the room without falling." The more I reward the outcome and the less I reward my guess about how to achieve it, the less I'm smuggling my own biases in. Shaping rewards are tempting because they speed up learning, but every shaping term is a place where I've told the agent how I think the problem should be solved, and I'm often wrong about that.

The second layer is adversarial. Before I run anything, I sit down and try to be the agent. If I were a lazy, infinitely clever optimizer, how would I get this number up without doing the thing? If the reward is "distance traveled," can I just vibrate? If it's "time the object is in the target region," can I knock it in there and then hold it so nothing else matters? Every one of those exploits I find on paper is one I don't have to discover after a week of compute.

The third layer, and this is where the field has moved, is admitting that for a lot of tasks I can't write the function at all. I know a good outcome when I see it, but I can't specify it. That's where you bring in preferences, demonstrations, learned reward models, and now increasingly language models as judges. You're still conveying intent through a reward, but you're letting the reward itself be learned from examples of what you mean, instead of hand-coding it. The risk just moves. Now the question is whether the learned reward generalizes the way your intent does, and usually it doesn't, so you need to keep humans in the loop to catch where it drifts.

If I had to compress all of that into one idea: the reward function isn't the specification. It's a lossy proxy for a specification that lives in your head. Design it knowing it's lossy, test it adversarially, and keep checking the agent's behavior against the thing you actually wanted, not against the number.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes reward functions as a way of conveying intent to an agent, while noting that this communication is lossy.

r002.rationale: It discusses specifying outcomes and learning rewards from examples, but does not state that verifiable tasks can communicate good performance without an explicit reward function.

r003.rationale: It says people may recognize a good outcome and should keep humans involved, but does not state that communicating good versus bad behavior requires tacit human common sense.

astra-6.text:
I think a reward function is a way of expressing what you want, but it’s usually an incomplete one. You have some intention—“I want the agent to do a good job”—and then you have to turn that into something you can measure. And there’s a gap between those two things.

For example, if you reward an assistant for getting a thumbs-up, you probably intend to reward helpfulness. But it might learn that agreeing with you gets a thumbs-up, even when you’re wrong. It has improved the measured outcome without necessarily doing what you wanted.

So I’d think about reward design as an iterative process. You propose a signal, see what behavior it produces, and ask where that behavior diverges from your intention. The important question isn’t just, “Does this reward good behavior?” It’s also, “What else could an agent do to earn this reward?”

r001.rationale: It describes a reward function as expressing what you want the agent to do and discusses how the agent’s behavior may diverge from that intention.

r002.rationale: It does not state that verifiable tasks can communicate good performance without an explicit reward function.

r003.rationale: It does not say that communicating good and bad behavior requires tacit human common sense.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a reward function is a way of communicating what you want, but it’s usually an incomplete way. You have some intention in your head, and then you write down a number that you hope captures that intention. The agent optimizes the number; it doesn’t necessarily understand everything you meant by it.

For example, if you reward an agent for finishing a task quickly, you probably also mean, “Do it correctly, don’t break anything, and ask me if something is ambiguous.” But unless those things are represented somehow, speed can come at their expense.

So I’d think of designing a reward function as an iterative process. You specify something, look at the behavior it produces, and ask where that behavior differs from what you intended. And sometimes the right fix isn’t another reward term. It might be a constraint, better feedback, or giving the agent a way to ask for clarification. The reward is part of the communication, rather than a complete specification of what you want.

r001.rationale: It describes a reward function as a way to communicate intended behavior to an agent, while noting that it may not capture the full intention.

r002.rationale: It does not say that verifiable tasks can communicate good performance without an explicit reward function.

r003.rationale: It mentions unstated expectations and ambiguity, but does not state that communicating good versus bad behavior requires tacit human common sense.
